subtopics.title: Overview of Computer Graphics & Software Standards
subtopics.subtitle: What graphics is, where it is used, coordinate systems, graphics packages and standards

concepts.text: What Computer Graphics Is

Computer graphics is the creation, storage and manipulation of pictures and models of objects using a computer. A graphics system converts a description of a scene (points, lines, polygons, curves, surfaces, colours) into an image on an output device such as a monitor or printer. It is distinct from image processing, which starts from an existing image and analyses or enhances it, although the two fields share hardware and many techniques.

rows: Drafting and modelling of buildings, circuits, machine parts, cars and aircraft
Scientific and business data shown as plots, charts, contour and volume images
Films, animation, special effects and computer games
Windows, icons, menus and pointers (WIMP) on every desktop and phone
Flight and driving simulators, virtual reality environments
Enhancing, restoring and analysing photographs, medical and satellite images
Interactive teaching models, digital painting and computer art

concepts.text: Interactive vs Passive Graphics
Graphics systems are classified by whether the user can control the picture:
items: Passive (non-interactive) graphics: the user has no control over the image once it is produced, e.g. a printed chart, a TV title sequence or a plotted drawing.
Interactive graphics: the user controls content, structure and appearance of the picture through input devices, with fast feedback, e.g. CAD, games, flight simulators and GUIs.

Interactive systems need three parts working together: a digital memory or frame buffer holding the image, a display monitor, and a display controller that passes the frame-buffer contents to the monitor.

concepts.text: Components of a complete graphics system:
items: Hardware: host CPU, display processor or GPU, frame buffer (video memory), video controller, display device, input devices and hard-copy output devices.
Software: the application program, a graphics package or API (OpenGL, DirectX), and device drivers that talk to the hardware.
Data: the application model or display file describing the objects to be drawn.

concepts.text: Coordinate Representations

Objects are first described in modelling (local) coordinates convenient for each shape. They are placed together in a single scene in world coordinates, a device-independent Cartesian frame. The scene is then mapped to normalized device coordinates (NDC), usually in the range 0 to 1 (or -1 to 1 in OpenGL), and finally to device coordinates, the integer pixel positions of a particular screen or printer. Keeping NDC as an intermediate step makes the package independent of the output device.
Graphics Software
Graphics software falls into two broad classes:
items: Special-purpose application packages: designed for non-programmers working in one area, e.g. AutoCAD, painting programs, charting tools and animation systems. The user works through menus without knowing how the drawing is done.

General-purpose programming packages: a library of graphics functions called from a language such as C or C++, e.g. GKS, PHIGS, OpenGL. The programmer builds any picture from primitives; such a package is also called a computer-graphics application programming interface (API).

concepts.text: Functions provided by a general-purpose graphics package:
items: Output primitives: the basic building blocks such as points, lines, polygons, circles, curves and character strings.
Attributes: properties of primitives such as colour, line width and style, fill pattern and text font.
Geometric and modelling transformations: translate, rotate and scale objects.
Viewing transformations: select a view of the scene, clip it to a window and map it to a viewport on the device.
Input functions: accept data from interactive devices such as a mouse, tablet or keyboard.
Control operations: housekeeping such as initialising the system, opening windows and clearing the screen.

concepts.text: Graphics Standards

rows: Graphical Kernel System: first ISO graphics standard (1985), 2D, device-independent
Programmer's Hierarchical Interactive Graphics System: 3D, objects stored as hierarchical structures that can be edited
PHIGS extended with lighting, shading and surface rendering
Computer Graphics Metafile: ISO file format for storing and transferring pictures between systems
Open, cross-platform 2D/3D API derived from SGI's GL (1992), now maintained by the Khronos Group
Microsoft's multimedia API family for Windows and Xbox; Direct3D is its 3D part
Khronos low-overhead, explicit API (2016) giving programs close control of the GPU

concepts.text: The OpenGL rendering pipeline in outline:
items: Vertex specification: the program sends vertex positions, colours, normals and texture coordinates.
Vertex processing: the vertex shader applies modelling, viewing and projection transformations.
Primitive assembly, clipping, perspective division and the viewport transformation to window coordinates.
Rasterisation: each primitive is converted into fragments (candidate pixels).
Fragment processing: the fragment shader computes colour, texturing and lighting per fragment.
Per-fragment operations: depth test, stencil test and blending, then the result is written to the frame buffer.

Normalized device coordinates are what make a graphics package device-independent: the same NDC picture can be scaled to any screen resolution or printer.
Do not confuse computer graphics (synthesising images from models) with image processing (operating on existing images); MCQs often use the distinction.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between interactive and passive computer graphics?
flashcards.back: In interactive graphics the user controls the picture through input devices with immediate feedback; in passive graphics the user cannot change the image once produced.

flashcards.front: Name the coordinate systems a point passes through from object description to screen.
flashcards.back: Modelling (local) coordinates, world coordinates, normalized device coordinates, then device (pixel) coordinates.
The Computer Graphics Metafile, an ISO standard file format for storing and exchanging device-independent pictures.

questions.questionText: Which was the first graphics software standard adopted by ISO?
questions.explanation: The Graphical Kernel System (GKS), a 2D device-independent package, was adopted by ISO in 1985; PHIGS and CGM followed later and OpenGL is an industry API.

questions.questionText: The graphics standard whose name refers to storing objects as editable hierarchical structures is:
questions.explanation: PHIGS (Programmer's Hierarchical Interactive Graphics System) organises object descriptions into a hierarchy of structures that can be modified and re-displayed.

questions.questionText: In the viewing pipeline, which coordinate system is used so that the picture description is independent of any particular output device?
questions.explanation: Normalized device coordinates (typically 0 to 1) are an intermediate, device-independent representation that is later scaled to the pixel coordinates of each device.

subtopics.title: Display Technology: Raster-Scan & Vector Displays
subtopics.subtitle: CRT basics, frame buffers, raster vs vector displays, colour CRTs and flat panels

concepts.text: The Cathode-Ray Tube

In a CRT an electron gun (heated cathode and control grid) emits a beam of electrons, which focusing and accelerating anodes direct at the phosphor-coated screen. Deflection plates (electrostatic) or deflection coils (magnetic) steer the beam horizontally and vertically. Where the beam strikes, the phosphor glows; the control grid voltage sets the beam intensity and hence the brightness of the spot.
Why the picture must be refreshed:
items: Persistence: the time for light emitted by the phosphor to decay to one-tenth of its original intensity. Low-persistence phosphors need frequent refreshing but suit animation; high-persistence phosphors suit static, complex pictures.
Refresh rate: the number of times per second the picture is redrawn. Below roughly 50 to 60 Hz the eye sees flicker; raster monitors typically use 60 to 80 Hz or more.
Resolution: the maximum number of points that can be displayed without overlap, usually quoted as horizontal pixels x vertical pixels (e.g. 1920 x 1080).

concepts.text: Raster-Scan Displays

In a raster-scan display the beam sweeps the whole screen one horizontal scan line at a time from top to bottom, turning the intensity on and off to form a pattern of pixels. The intensity or colour of every pixel is held in a memory area called the frame buffer (refresh buffer). Because the picture is a grid of pixels, raster displays can show shaded, filled and realistic images, but sloping lines show jagged steps (aliasing).
Retrace and interlacing:
items: Horizontal retrace: at the end of each scan line the beam returns to the left edge of the next line with the beam turned off.
Vertical retrace: after the last scan line the beam returns to the top-left corner to start the next frame.

Interlacing: odd-numbered lines are drawn in one pass (field) and even-numbered lines in the next, so the whole screen is covered twice per frame. A 30 frame/s picture then refreshes at 60 fields/s, reducing flicker at lower bandwidth.

concepts.plainText: Frame buffer size = H x V x n bits (n = bits per pixel)

concepts.text: Colour depth, lookup tables and aspect ratio:
items: With n bits per pixel (n bit planes) a pixel can take 2^n distinct values: 1 bit gives black and white (bitmap), 8 bits give 256 colours, 24 bits give 16,777,216 colours.
Colour lookup table: pixel values index a table of full-colour entries, e.g. 8-bit pixels select 256 simultaneous colours from a palette of 2^24 held as 24-bit table entries.
Aspect ratio: the ratio of horizontal to vertical size of the display (e.g. 4:3, 16:9), or of the number of vertical points to horizontal points needed to draw equal-length lines.

concepts.text: Random-Scan (Vector) Displays

A random-scan or vector display directs the beam only to the parts of the screen where the picture is drawn, tracing each line directly from one endpoint to the other like a pen plotter. The picture is stored as a set of line-drawing commands called the display file (display list or refresh display file). The display processor cycles through these commands 30 to 60 times per second; lines are smooth with no staircase effect, but filled areas and realistic shading are not possible.

rows: Fixed pattern, every line of the screen
Only along the lines to be drawn
Pixel intensities in a frame buffer
Line commands in a display file
Grows with the number of lines

concepts.text: Colour CRTs and Flat-Panel Displays
Two ways a CRT produces colour:
items: Beam penetration: two phosphor layers (red outside, green inside); the beam speed decides how far electrons penetrate. Only four colours (red, green, orange, yellow) are possible; cheap and used with random-scan systems.

Shadow mask: three electron guns (red, green, blue) and a screen of RGB phosphor dot triads; a metal shadow mask with one hole per triad ensures each beam hits only its own colour. It gives a wide range of colours and is used in raster-scan colour monitors.

concepts.text: Flat-panel technologies:
items: LCD: liquid crystal between polarisers twists light to pass or block it; it is non-emissive and needs a backlight. TN panels are fast and cheap but have narrow viewing angles; IPS panels give better colour and wide viewing angles.

Passive-matrix LCD: pixels are addressed at the crossings of row and column conductors, which is cheap but slow with lower contrast. Active-matrix LCD: a thin-film transistor (TFT) at each pixel holds its state, giving faster response and better contrast.
LED display: either an LCD with an LED backlight, or a direct-view panel of light-emitting diodes (large outdoor screens).
OLED: organic layers emit light at each pixel, so no backlight is needed, blacks are true black, contrast is very high and panels can be thin or flexible.
Plasma: cells of neon-based gas between electrode grids glow when ionised; emissive and bright, used for large screens, but heavy and power-hungry.

rows: Cost, burn-in, ageing of blue pixels

formulas.plainText: Frame buffer (bytes) = H x V x n / 8
Number of colours = 2^n for n bits per pixel
Horizontal scan rate = number of scan lines x refresh rate (ignoring retrace)

notes.text: For frame-buffer questions multiply resolution by bits per pixel, divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for KB and again for MB: 1024 x 768 x 24 / 8 = 2,359,296 bytes = 2.25 MB.
Raster = frame buffer of pixels, aliasing, fixed scan pattern; vector = display file of line commands, smooth lines, no filled areas. Swapping these is the classic MCQ trap.
Beam penetration gives only four colours and pairs with random-scan displays; the shadow mask with three guns is the method used in colour raster monitors.

formulas.title: Frame-buffer size
formulas.plainText: Size (bytes) = H x V x n / 8
formulas.description: Memory needed to store one full screen of H by V pixels at n bits per pixel.

formulas.title: Colours from bit depth
formulas.description: Number of distinct values a pixel can hold with n bits per pixel.

formulas.title: Horizontal scan rate
formulas.description: Scan lines drawn per second, ignoring retrace time, e.g. 768 x 60 = 46,080 lines/s.

formulas.title: Aspect ratio
formulas.description: Ratio of horizontal to vertical size of the display, e.g. 1920 / 1080 = 16:9.

flashcards.back: The time taken for light emitted by the phosphor to decay to one-tenth of its original intensity after the beam leaves.

flashcards.front: What is interlacing in a raster display?
flashcards.back: Drawing odd scan lines in one field and even lines in the next, so the screen is refreshed twice per frame and flicker is reduced.

flashcards.front: How does an active-matrix LCD differ from a passive-matrix LCD?
flashcards.back: An active-matrix LCD has a thin-film transistor at every pixel to hold its state, giving faster response and better contrast than passive row-column addressing.

flashcards.front: Why can a vector display not show filled, shaded areas?
flashcards.back: It stores and draws only line commands from its display file, tracing lines directly, so it has no pixel memory for area shading.

questions.questionText: What frame-buffer memory is required for a 1280 x 1024 raster display with 24 bits per pixel?
A raster system has 8 bit planes per pixel. How many colours can it display simultaneously?
questions.explanation: With n bits per pixel a pixel can take 2^n values, so 2^8 = 256 simultaneous colours.

questions.questionText: In an active-matrix LCD, what is placed at each pixel to control and hold its state?
questions.explanation: Active-matrix (TFT) LCDs put a transistor at every pixel; shadow masks and phosphor triads belong to colour CRTs and gas cells to plasma panels.

subtopics.title: Display Processors, Input & Output Devices
subtopics.subtitle: Raster and random-scan architectures, display processors, GPUs, input and output devices

concepts.text: Raster-Scan System Architecture

A simple raster system connects the CPU, system memory, a video controller and I/O devices to the system bus. The frame buffer may be a fixed area of system memory or separate video memory; the video controller has direct access to it so it can refresh the screen without involving the CPU. The CPU runs the application and writes pixel values, while the video controller continuously reads them out to the monitor.
How the video controller refreshes the screen:
items: Two registers hold the current pixel's x and y; starting at the top-left, the controller fetches the pixel value from the frame buffer and uses it to set the beam intensity.
x is incremented along the scan line; at the end of the line x is reset and y moves to the next line; after the last line both are reset for the next frame.
To keep up, several pixels are fetched in one memory access and held in a shift register.
Extra features: colour lookup tables, double buffering (draw into one buffer while the other is displayed, then swap) for smooth animation, and zooming or panning.

concepts.text: More capable systems add a display processor (graphics controller or display coprocessor) with its own display-processor memory. Its main job is scan conversion: digitising a picture definition from the application into pixel values in the frame buffer, e.g. drawing lines, circles, filled polygons and characters. It also performs raster operations such as bit-block transfers (BitBLT), pattern filling, antialiasing and, in many designs, clipping and transformations, freeing the CPU from graphics work.

concepts.plainText: Pixel rate = H x V x refresh rate (pixels per second, ignoring retrace)

concepts.text: Random-Scan System Architecture

In a random-scan system the application program and graphics package translate drawing commands into a display file stored in system memory. The display processor, sometimes called the display processing unit or graphics controller, fetches and executes these commands one by one, driving the deflection system so the beam traces each line. It cycles through the whole display file once per refresh, typically 30 to 60 times per second.

A modern graphics processing unit (GPU) is the descendant of the display processor: a massively parallel processor with thousands of simple cores and its own high-bandwidth video memory. It runs the whole rendering pipeline in hardware, executing programmable vertex and fragment shaders, rasterisation, texturing, depth testing and blending, and is also used for general-purpose parallel computing such as machine learning.
Input Devices

rows: Relative motion from a ball or optical sensor, plus buttons
Ball rotated by hand in a fixed housing
Pointing where desk space is limited
Stick tilted from a centre position
Stylus or puck position sensed on a grid
Photocell detects the CRT beam passing under its tip
Resistive, capacitive, optical or acoustic sensing of a finger
Optical scanning of paper into a digital image
Sensors measure hand and finger positions
Grasping and moving objects in virtual reality
Selection from a list of options
Light pen, mouse click on object

concepts.text: Output Devices
Printers are divided by whether they strike the paper:
items: Impact printers press formed characters or pins against an inked ribbon onto paper: dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and line printers. They are noisy but can print multi-part forms.

Non-impact printers form the image without striking the paper: laser printers (a laser charges a drum that picks up toner), inkjet printers (fine ink droplets), thermal and dye-sublimation printers. They are quieter and give higher quality.

concepts.text: Other hard-copy and immersive output devices:
items: Pen plotters: flatbed or drum (roller) plotters move pens along the paper to draw vector lines, used for large engineering drawings; raster plotters use electrostatic or inkjet methods.
3D printers: build a solid object layer by layer (additive manufacturing) from a 3D model, e.g. fused deposition modelling, stereolithography or selective laser sintering.
VR headsets: a head-mounted display shows a separate image to each eye for stereoscopic depth and tracks head movement so the view updates as the user turns.

formulas.plainText: Time per pixel = 1 / (H x V x refresh rate)
Video bandwidth = H x V x refresh rate x n/8 bytes per second

notes.text: Remember the six logical input classes by what they return: locator (a point), stroke (many points), string (text), valuator (a number), choice (an option), pick (an object).

The video controller only reads the frame buffer to refresh the screen; the display processor writes into it by scan-converting primitives. In random-scan systems the display processor instead executes the display file directly.
A light pen works by detecting the CRT electron beam, so it does not work on LCD panels; a touch screen, not a light pen, is the modern way to point directly at the display.

formulas.title: Pixel rate
formulas.plainText: Pixel rate = H x V x refresh rate
formulas.description: Number of pixels the video controller must read out per second, ignoring retrace.

formulas.title: Time per pixel
formulas.plainText: t_pixel = 1 / (H x V x refresh rate)
formulas.description: Upper bound on the time available to fetch and display each pixel.

formulas.title: Video memory bandwidth
formulas.plainText: B = H x V x refresh rate x n/8 bytes per second
formulas.description: Bytes per second the frame buffer must supply to refresh the screen at n bits per pixel.

flashcards.back: Digitising a picture definition (lines, circles, polygons) into the set of pixel values stored in the frame buffer; it is the main task of a raster display processor.

flashcards.front: What does a pick logical input device return?
flashcards.back: The identification of a displayed object or picture component the user has selected, e.g. by pointing with a light pen or mouse.
The next frame is drawn into a back buffer while the front buffer is displayed, then they are swapped, so animation appears without flicker or tearing.

questions.questionText: Which logical input device class supplies a single scalar value, such as a setting read from a dial or slider?
questions.explanation: A valuator returns a real number; a locator returns one coordinate position, a stroke a sequence of positions and a pick an identified object.

questions.questionText: A 1024 x 768 raster display is refreshed at 60 Hz. Ignoring retrace, about how much time is available to display each pixel?
questions.explanation: Pixel rate = 1024 x 768 x 60 = 47,185,920 pixels/s, so time per pixel = 1 / 47,185,920, about 21.2 ns.

questions.questionText: Which input device senses the electron beam of a CRT as it passes under its tip to locate a point on the screen?
questions.explanation: A light pen contains a photocell that detects the burst of light when the CRT beam refreshes the spot under it, so the system can tell where it is pointing.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an impact printer?
questions.explanation: A dot-matrix printer strikes pins against an inked ribbon onto the paper; laser, inkjet and thermal printers form the image without striking the paper.
